slides: Open with the chapter question rather than the equation. A projective conic is a quadratic locus, but in this lecture it also functions as a copy of P^1 inside the plane. The deck follows the notebook arc from parametrization to invariants, incidence theorems, polarity, intersections, and pencils.

Use this slide as a translation table for the rest of the lecture. The point is that almost every geometric construction in the chapter has a small linear algebra representative: points and lines are vectors, incidence is a dot product, conics are symmetric matrices, and projective motion is conjugation of the matrix.

Spend time on why the parameter is the main object. The displayed affine circle is only one chart of the projective conic; the formula with u gives every finite parameter and the extra point at infinity closes the projective line. The residual check keeps the parametrization honest.

Present cross-ratio as the invariant that lets the conic inherit one-dimensional projective geometry. The two rows in the table are deliberately different parameter values, yet the computed number is the same to floating point precision. This is the bridge from a curve in the plane to P^1 arithmetic.

This slide explains why parametrization is not merely a convenient plotting trick. Once a conic is identified with P^1, a projectivity preserving it acts by a fractional linear change of parameter. Conversely, parameter motion predicts how marked points on the conic must move under a plane projectivity.

State Pascal as an incidence theorem and then immediately point to the computational pipeline. The theorem does not depend on a regular hexagon or metric symmetry; it is about six arbitrary conic points in projective position. The notebook image uses uneven parameters so the collinearity is not hidden by symmetry.

Use the determinant formula to make Pascal feel executable. The construction is join, meet, join, then one incidence test. This is also a good moment to remind students that homogeneous coordinates keep points at infinity inside the same algebra rather than forcing separate exceptional cases.

Emphasize the dual role of the conic matrix. The same Q that evaluates the quadratic equation also sends a point to a line. On the conic that line is tangent; off the conic it is polar. Symmetry of Q is the reason the incidence relation works in both directions.

Frame Bezout as a stability statement rather than only an intersection-count slogan. A real affine drawing can hide complex points or points at infinity, but the projective complex count remains four when multiplicity is included and no component is shared. The selected example keeps all four points visible for inspection.

Explain pencils as linear algebra families of conics. The parameter lambda moves through a projective line of quadratic forms, and determinant zero marks the moments when rank drops. The saved interactive artifact lets students watch smooth conics pass through singular members instead of treating degeneracy as an error.

The lab reverses the usual direction of the chapter. Five points impose five linear conditions on the six conic coefficients, leaving one projective solution in the generic case. After fitting, a projective change of coordinates must move both the points and the matrix compatibly, which the residuals verify.

Use the pitfalls slide to slow down before the recap. The safest computational habit is to keep homogeneous coordinates until the final drawing step. Normalizing too early, ignoring infinity, or trusting a real affine picture can erase exactly the projective features the chapter is designed to preserve.

Close by collecting the lecture into reusable certificates. Parametrization certifies membership, cross-ratio certifies projective invariance, Pascal certifies collinearity, polarity certifies tangent incidence, Bezout certifies stable intersection count, and the pencil determinant certifies singular members. The common habit is to translate geometry into a checkable homogeneous statement.
